question.prompt: A poll shows that \(70\%\) of all voters approve of the mayor’s work. On three separate occasions a pollster selects a voter at random. What is the probability that on exactly one of these three occasions the voter approves of the mayor’s work?

solutions.explanation:
Assume first that the three selections are independent and that the approval probability remains \(0.70\), as in the intended model. Write \(A\) for approval and \(D\) for nonapproval. Exactly one approval can occur in precisely three orders:
\[
ADD,\qquad DAD,\qquad DDA.
\]
The nonapproval probability is \(1-0.70=0.30\). By independence, each listed order has probability
\[
0.70\cdot0.30\cdot0.30=0.063.
\]
The three orders are disjoint and include every way to obtain exactly one approval. Their total probability is therefore
\[
3\cdot0.063=\boxed{0.189},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\) under this assumption.

Independence is essential, however, and separate occasions alone do not explicitly specify it. For a counterexample, suppose there are ten voters, seven approving and three nonapproving, and the pollster selects three different voters at random without replacement. Each of the same three approval orders has probability \((7\cdot3\cdot2)/(10\cdot9\cdot8)\): the factors count one approving voter and two distinct nonapproving voters in the specified order. Thus the probability is
\[
3\cdot\frac7{10}\cdot\frac39\cdot\frac28
=\frac7{40}=0.175.
\]
This population also has \(70\%\) approval but gives a different answer. Hence \(0.189\), choice B, is justified by the independent-selection interpretation; the displayed conditions alone do not determine a unique probability.
solutions.title: List the three approval orders and check the assumption
